I sincerely cannot recommend this game, though I desperately want to. What is this game, exactly? It's Creeper World meets a base development/unit RTS like Riftbreaker. In Creeper World the enemy is the ever-flowing, never stopping Creep. In that game, pacing is everything. That's precisely what's missing in Glory to Goo: pacing. Here the "Creep" is merely unclaimed territory that makes unit adventuring dangerous and building impossible. There is no inherent danger from the Creep. Once territory is claimed, it's essentially yours barring a serious base failure. The danger in G2G comes from periodic mob rushes which are usually tame. As such, the mid-game and late-game has serious pacing issues. Gotta build more power generators? Need to build a thumper to get land to do so. Wait 45 secs for it to build to get 5x5 of territory. Then build more generators. Rinse, repeat. A lot of these issues could be solved by contextual queueing of the construction UI. Creeper World does this and also allows many buildings to physically move themselves onto new territory. That's how CW solved mid and late game pacing issues. G2G needs something similar. As it stands, G2G gets very grindy and repetitive about 20 min into a scenario. There's a lot of unpolished balancing and good ideas in the game: such as having your orbital mothership provide support on the ground. However, that idea needs a bit of rework (it's a little clunky in action). Like, what's the point of workforce generators on the ship? To make ship upgrades faster? To shave off 30 secs of upgrade time? 30 secs could be a lifetime in Creeper World and be the difference in victory, but in G2G that's.... listen, an entire scenario is going to be 5 hours long. 30 secs means nothing at all in context. How come the base on the planet doesn't have that? Like, a building/upgrade that doesn't change the total resources a construction needs but just does building faster? Where the hell is that? There is a building that kinda does that at the furthest end of the tech tree... but it is needed by the player about 2 hours before that point to shave off almost half-hours of gameplay lost on waiting for construction. Oh... and walls are useless. For a game about tower defense and building... if a bunker costs the same as 5 walls and "walls" off more than actual walls... players will just spam bunkers. Riftbreaker does this idea right with mass production queueing of walls that are cheap, but you could splurge on the expensive walls for real defense. No. In G2G, there's just one type of wall and bunkers are less expensive and more useful. The game also clearly wants you to go adventuring with your commander outside of the confines of the base. That's effectively suicide. Units are too expensive to lose willy nilly. Riftbreaker does this idea right by making adventuring -TOO FAR- from base as suicide, but also adds in real rewards for that risk. The best result of such a venture in G2G is you find a node to increase research production... but will probably lose half your units in the process for even venturing a screen away from your base limits. Lots of good ideas here. But the game is a slog. Buy Riftbreaker or any of the Creeper Worlds instead.

It's true this game is a lot like They are Billions but with seemingly more eventual paths and upgrades. However, this game is crippled by its pixel graphics in my opinion. All of the human units look basically the same at the middle zoom level. They are almost all blue sprays of pixels. All of the aliens look the same at the middle zoom level, they are purple sprays of pixels. Yes, there are a couple red or grey variations, but once you hit 20 clumped units, you can't tell what units are where. The robot faction is similarly uniform. Imagine if, in starcraft, M&M was the only way for any faction to play and the drop ships also look like floating marines. This probably wont bother most people, but for those people who want to set up squads and micro units, I don't think it's good.

[h1]A bit meh[/h1] I’ll name a few games that may be similar to this one and point out what feels off in GFTG: Age of Empires? Bad UI, boring strategy, no meaningful starting choices. StarCraft? Too slow. Cossacks? Yes, lots of units, but the game is slow and punishing. They Are Billions? Bad UI, weak visuals, no QoL features, no tension, no real “power mode.” Creeper World? Too shallow. Too grindy. Overall, it feels like the devs had a solid idea but lacked the experience to execute it properly. This game manages to bundle together everything that doesn’t quite work. Too slow for a fast-paced RTS. Too grindy for an RPG. Too shallow in terms of UI/UX. What’s left is closer to a technical demo of “we’ve put some features together,” but forgot to make it actually fun. Even if this is Early Access, why would you pay for a product that feels this raw? Feels like the foundation is there—but the house was never finished.

EDIT: The developer has responded to this review and is addressing the difficulty curve, and has been courteous and professional in their response. I'll rewrite this review when I get back into the game. This game was really fun for the first several hours, then ramped up difficulty to an extreme even on easy mode. Swarms are too frequent and massive to give you any kind of chance to build up defense and an army, so making progress on missions is excruciatingly slow. If you just barely manage to survive one wave, there's absolutely no chance you're going to survive the next one a few minutes later. It also does a terrible job of explaining or even showing mechanics, so I had no idea I needed to be doing things to set myself up for success in later missions. Trying to manage your ship, your captain, the base defenses, and making offensive attacks is insanely difficult, and even as someone pretty familiar with the RTS genre, it's just too much. I've tried replaying the same mission over and over, with a different strategy every time, and nothing works. I've given up. Feels like the rug was pulled out from from under me because I played too long to get a refund.

I have had this game in my library for quite a long time. I have played on and off but never got to the campaign, how good could it be? I was extremely surprised how the campaign has turned out so far, the dialogue is pleasant and engaging but what most impresses me is the R&D and investment strategies you are asked to apply. Regions you gain control of tend to have an optional "boost" you have to select and will impact how you play. This choice is static throughout the game so you live with it long term. But, there is also extreme flexibility in the upgrade system for your units and buildings. Think of them as toggles. Turn tech on and off. You want this tech for this mission? ALLOCATE resources towards that tech. But if the next mission you don't need that specific tech, then REALLOCATE it to another tech. This really tailors the buffs to YOUR playing style -- turtling, rushing, econ-stomp, etc. The factions are asymmetric in their play-style. Very well done. It's NOT just how units behave or perform. It's the expansion, logistics, defense and planning of it all. Having your assistant space ship in orbit is also a great addition to the game. It can be a logistics supply line or a gunship of death. Click and DRAG the minigun path. Don't individual click like I did, you'll blow your eardrums. :p If you can get past the pixel graphics and enjoy RTS with some board-game like elements thrown in, you will love this game. Also, you can pause nearly any time. If you're reflexes or eyes aren't as good as they once were, pausing makes this game so well paced. Great job. I am looking forward to updates and hopefully a sequel that keeps the charm of the game but goes for some more fidelity (units really should be way more visibly distinct and you can only do so much at this pixel count and scale.

Great RTS with a ton of replayability and customizability. Has a ton of cool concepts, like artillery and anti air, different types of meta progression including unit variations and different factions and a spaceship that you develop alongside your base and can support you in various ways. I also really appreciate the simplicity and the fact that you simply mine and use your resources, instead of going the Factorio way of endless processing, I really hope this does not change in the future. It clearly is an early access game and it sometimes shows, with small things like buildings Z fighting, units getting unselected, enemies not getting hit while out of bounds or in water and a bunch of other small things, but I've never encountered anything remotely gamebreaking. With the developer adding new content, like the campaign, it's a steal. Looking forward to more content.
